Ctdas8WvPSg.content:
Celebrating a big win today. 💖

I finally found a psychologist who doesn’t just specialise in Bipolar Disorder (win!) but has ticked off most of the other requirements I felt I needed to support my mental well-being. (Big win!!) 

I feel relieved, I feel excited. 

I haven’t even seen her yet but the warmth and inclusivity I feel from our email exchanges makes me feel hopeful. Makes me feel excited to know that I will have the support I need going forward. 

It feels like a new chapter. 
A year ago, my mental health/bipolar was at its absolute worst. 
I felt untethered, and overwhelmed and purposeless. I felt unloved and worthless.
I felt like a burden. 

I had a very severe mental breakdown. I lost a lot of people who I thought were close to me. I found some people who took me seriously and supported my mental health and recovery. 
It took the last 6 months of getting me onto the right meds and for the side effects to wear off. 
It took 9 months to get into a hospital program to learn the skills to support myself. (And 3 months for the waiting period!)
It took a year to believe I’m worth it and I deserve happiness. 
Finding my new therapist feels like the final piece of the puzzle.
Finding a human who wants to be apart of my support team, who wants to see
me succeed, and in her words ‘cultivate a full and meaningful life’ 

Bipolar will always be with me but it won’t get to always take the best of me.

Amazing resource from @bipolarexplained about Bipolar Disorder and loneliness.

The trigger that we may not be enough setting off our abandonment trauma or the myriad of other traumas, PLUS having the predisposition for disregulated emotions is bad news for us. Understanding Bipolar/mental health both as a person with it or as a friend/support person works wonders for avoiding/stalling the descent into depression and loneliness and supporting us through our growth out of it.

Ct_exHrvZ9J.content:
Mentally, I’m here. I was in Albany over the weekend and I happened to spot the whales as they are migrating. 
It was a pretty great grounding moment. 

See, It’s been a tough week as I’ve been in the midst of a Mixed Episode. 

A mixed episode in Bipolar is when you experience both Depression and Hypomania (or mania for BP1) at the same time. 

Symptoms can include:

-feeling a mixture of elevated and low moods
-doing pleasurable activities but still having depressive symptoms
-experiencing low mood with rapid speech
-experiencing elevated mood with suicidal ideation
-experiencing severely disturbed sleep
-having a severe disruption of appetite

Amongst my peers we call this time ‘tired but wired’. 

In my own experience I’ve felt my heart racing, but I’m tired AF. 
I have trouble falling to sleep but then I sleep 9+ hrs. 
I experience Anhedonia. An inability to experience pleasure from activities I usually find enjoyable. 
Additionally my social battery is incredibly low. 
I have severe generalised anxiety and intrusive and/or ruminating thoughts. 
I have trouble articulating myself, but also stumble through a giant overshare. 
I get easily distracted and confused. 
I get very easily overwhelmed and cry a lot over the (depressed) pain I’m in. 

The best I can do in this situation is to be aware of my mood and do my best to avoid triggering or stimulating activities. I primarily distract myself with low effort activities and tasks. 

I limit my social media interactions and try to organise a few fulfilling but low effort social activities. 

Mainly I’ve been crawled up with a book and chocolate ✨ 

It will pass and I’ll return to my normal mood cycles, so I’ve just got to ride it out.

But in the meantime, I’m practicing my gratefulness. I found a profound moment of peace in this moment and I’m revisiting it as often as possible to soothe my nervous system. 

Peace ✌🏻 Tahlia

CwSLfx3vrMD.content:
What I love about Bipolar ⬆️ ⬇️ 

Not all of Bipolar is bad, whilst both the mood cycles (Hypomania and Depression) can be hard to manage there are some positives to my condition. 

💖 When the hypomanic days work for me. I can channel my power into being insanely productive, I get all my overdue tasks done, I clean the house, I finish that ‘thing that needs doing’. It makes up for the days of depression when I can barely make a meal for myself. 

💖 How happy I can feel. The euphoria of almost feeling love-drunk without the actual drunk part. 🤪 How the sun feels on my skin, how beautiful the world is, how bright colours are, books become a magic adventure, movies are a thrilling escape, generally feeling a child-like wonder towards the world - I’ve been told the symptoms are similar to MDMA 😅

💖 Tied in with this is how deeply I can feel. It goes both ways, the depression can be so destructive but the love and empathy is so deeply connecting. I feel a deep love and connection to my family and friends, I feel another’s feelings as if they are my own, I cry for them, I laugh with them, but I can also deeply support another person with my level of emotional understanding. 💓

💖 The creativity I have. My mind goes wild with ideas. I want to cross-stitch, build a miniature model, do pottery, paint, draw, make something with my hands. I just itch to do something else that isn’t passive like watching TV, lately it’s been Rhine-stoning my Burly Costumes! 💎 

💖 I can help other babes with Bipolar. I have a passion and a drive to educate and help others deal with their own or a loved ones Bipolar. 

💋 Tahlia x

Hey, Hi, Hello! 👋 

There’s so many new faces here (hey there bots! 🤖) that I wanted to take this opportunity to reintroduce myself. 

Firstly, a bit about me:

✨ In my Thirties and Thriving ✌🏻 
✨ I’m happily married (and keep that private 💋) 
✨ I’m a dancer and burlesque performer 👠 
✨ I love expressing myself through makeup and fashion 💄 
✨ I’m a big ally and a safe space 🏳️‍🌈🏳️‍⚧️
✨ I’m a HUGE Sherlock fan, and no not just Benedict Cumberbatch (but Benny, feel free to call me anytime 📞 ) 

Secondly, this space is a bit of a personal blog, rather than my personal life. 

I may live day to day here but I’m not just another selfie queen on Instagram. In fact I’m strongly the opposite and I actively work to make Instagram a positive influence, by centering on the following:

💖Pro-Aging, Body Acceptance and Sexual Empowerment 💖

I have a new-found appreciation for being sexually empowered, unashamed and unapologetic. And I want to encourage others to feel that for themselves. You’ll NEVER see face/body altering filters here, that’s a promise. A toxic culture of unhealthy habits and mindsets took control of my teens/20s for too long, and I’m here to tell society f*ck that!
//F*ck anti-aging and F*ck bodies being a trend🖕🏻//

💖Mental Health: reducing stigma through education 💖

My main gig here (besides being a Comedy Queen 💁🏻‍♀️) is mental health awareness and education, Specifically Bipolar Disorder, as I’m formally diagnosed with Bipolar Disorder Type 2, and GAD.

There is so much information out there but what I don’t see is the in’s and out’s of everyday life with BP - understanding of the toughness and complexity of the disorder. So even when it’s ugly and tough and I think no one wants to hear my depressive stories, I share them. Because knowledge is power, and education begets progress. 

I also believe that Instagram has become the place for ‘highlight reels’, and I want to change that.
I want it to be the place for the REAL. No matter how uncomfortable or confronting. 

I’m multi-faceted. I’ll love you with my whole self. I’ll make a sex joke at the worst time. I’m flirtatious and depressing.

C0G-rAxv-zZ.content:
Remember what we grew up with? 
‘Cocaine thin’ models and Retouched & Airbrushed Cosmo and Dolly magazines? 

We didn’t even have technology to be in our face 24/7, and we STILL grew up with huge body image problems, eating disorders and ridiculous body standards. 

How do young people stand a chance with celebrities that can’t admit they’ve had work done? When there’s AI image filtering, FaceTune, face augmenting filters, clear skin filters, etc. distorting our interpretation of what we should look like? 

Social Media (primarily its ‘influencers’ - amongst other things) has contributed towards a toxic culture of being preoccupied with perceived defects and flaws contributing to an increase in cosmetic procedures to ‘fix’ these perceived flaws. 
These constant messages day-in day-out have a profound effect upon our youth. 

After battling some pretty heavy body image issues (what 00’s teen girl didn’t) I’m determined to have a positive effect on those who look up to me, and I hope you do too. 
 
Start by having easy conversations with your younger siblings, charges, or children.
Start by talking about yourself with a loving mindset. 
Start by following positive movements against beauty standards. 

I’ll start with this untouched photo of me, my fine lines, my zits and sunspots enjoying a Moana Icecream at Disneyworld. 

I will love you more for being you than you trying to be anyone else, I promise x

C8g3T34vXlc.content:
PART ONE ☝🏻
 
This post is SO overdue, but I’ve been busy growing two humans. 😅

This year I ticked a big one off the bucket list. My first Burlesque Solo. 
It had been coming for a while but I finally committed to the 6week Sugar Blue Solo Act Course. 
There was no turning back now. In just over 6 weeks I was gonna perform on stage an original number from a lil idea in my head. 

Then? I found out I was pregnant. 

WOOF. 🐶 

The first week I thought I was gonna quit. 
This was too overwhelming and my imposter syndrome kicked in BIG time. I’m a dancer not a choreographer! How was I gonna come up with a WHOLE ROUTINE???? How does one do that exactly? Plus making a costume? You wish! 
ALSO, throw in a quick crash course in ‘what to do when you’re having a baby’ in the background? How exactly am I gonna balance all this? 
I was sick with worry and at the same time felt a profound sense of shame. Quitting again? Typical. My confidence in myself and my abilities is so low, and I was saddened by the realisation that my anxiety is stronger than my belief in myself. 
I also knew this was perhaps my last time in a while I’d even get the opportunity, So the pressure was enormous. 
I was descending into a spiral of depression. 

[…cont in the next post]

C8g38Pdv3rq.content:
PART TWO. ✌🏻 

I can’t even remember now what happened, I wish I could tell you but I just remember that profound feeling of, ‘No. You will not quit again. You will prove to yourself that you can.’ I wanted to be someone who didn’t always quit, or be overwhelmed by my anxiety.

The creative rush came in ebbs and flows.
One session I came up with 2mins in one go! 2 mins? That’s half the routine! The pride In my accomplishment that day was the tonic to keep going. And other weeks (and I mean WEEKS) I was empty, when I had nothing. 

THEN, for plot twist number TWO… IT’S TWINS 😮😮 preoccupation with the big news also sidelined my impending project for another stretch 🤣

But by the day I was so ready. I was so proud of the piece I had put together. I knew it was good. And as always, being on stage is a different kind of rush. Performing is in my blood. That evening everything was stripped away and I felt, (like you always do!) that this thing you were terrified of gives you LIFE and you now want it all the time. I wanted to do this act every weekend, hell I wanted to create another!!!! Not to mention I was 13 weeks pregnant and proud as hell of my mumma-to-be self doing something AWESOME.

I miss Burly right now but I can’t wait to return and add another number to my repertoire. ❤️

DBX-M0FTdI_.content:
🎂 🎂 🎂 

Today is a birthday unlike any other in my life. This birthday I’m a mum. Of TWO. I’m a mum of twins. It’s still pretty surreal to say. I feel like me still, there are just two new tenants in this house that are incredibly demanding 😅

It’s been a tough two weeks. The adjustment was a huge slap to the face, any parent knows one child is demanding - two has been insanely hard. My first few days in hospital weren’t great, even though I was flagged as Bipolar (hence an at risk patient) with staffing issues and an overfull labour ward, I didn’t get any help to breastfeed or any sleep for 3 days. I slipped through the cracks in there system and my mental health took a very dangerous dive. I’m on the mend and thankfully had an uptick when the good midwives got me back on track, and I’ve had extra help at home from my mum (thank you mummy 💖) and my mother-in-law. 

I will say the birth was amazing. A twin birth vaginally is rare, so rare I didn’t realise til I was at the hospital. Every midwife had a look of shock on her face or gave me a ‘fuck yeah go you!!!’ - even the physio was confused when she checked for my scar and saw it had ‘healed miraculously’ 🤣 I was like ‘I didn’t have a c-section’ and she responded with excited expletives ☺️
I cried my eyes out when the student midwife at my delivery came to visit me days later and shared that she had told my story in class - about how it reminded her why she wants to be a midwife. 

I feel so proud I stuck to my guns with my choice to not get bullied into a Caesar. 

(Second) Last but not least, my husband, @bradequate  there is a whole post I could write about you. Your strength and support and love is unparalleled. I literally couldn’t have got through this without you. You pulled me from my darkest moments and lifted me up through my best. I love you. You’re already in an incredible Dad (DaddyBraddy/Dadley)

Lastly, thank you my babies for making me a mother for my birthday this year; I’m learning and growing as we take this wild ride together, twin life is gonna be so amazing once we get through this lil patch! But I already see so much personality in you both and you’re FREAKING ADORABLE!

💖 T x

DKEv4gIzXwC.content:
I participated in my last triathlon in 2015, Devonport, Tasmania. I left the sport after experiencing multiple stress fractures, chronic fatigue, and undergoing two surgeries for external iliac artery endofibrosis. 

On reflection, I can now say I was trying to compensate for something. Someone once asked me what was I running from? Honestly, at the time this puzzled me. I now appreciate their honesty. 

I had not yet learnt how to fuel my body to train, perform and recover. @danatk08 you did always say energy in vs energy out. I now understand this. 

Over the years I have maintained some level of fitness in rec running. But never had the drive to “Race” again. I had not yet found the “Why”. 

On a recent trip to Girona, Spain where @sallypilbeam and @steve_gleeson were based for the Paris Paralympic prep - safe to say was inspired. I had the opportunity to join for some run sessions with @sallypilbeam @charlottehall_hk & @steve_gleeson . I was reminded of how strong the mind and body is, most importantly how strong the human heart is.

Working as a Clinical Nurse Manager in Aged Care, I see on a daily basis what it’s like to live without your health and mobility. This is a strong motivator for me. 

With the help of my husband @steve_gleeson I have found the “Why”.

The mentors, coaches, and support network over the years who have played such a valuable role in not only developing athletes, but developing good people. 
For me, your advice has deeply impacted all aspects of my life. 

The art of showing up, staying disciplined & resilient, it’s priceless 🏃‍♀️✌️

YOUR ✨HOT MUM ERA✨ STARTS HERE 🩷

This is a space where we get to REMEMBER our POWER, and understand that motherhood gets to be our strongest era yet. It doesn’t have to keep bringing us down - motherhood was MEANT for us, to show us our weaknesses, in order to strengthen us more than we ever knew we could.

DYxfSNHknF1.content:
Hey 👋 I’M ALANA! 

Lately… I’ve been thinking about what I’m passionate about. And honestly? It’s been a bit of a journey to work out exactly what that is, but I think a really good way to figure it out is to ask yourself what you could literally talk underwater about. What you could chew someone’s ear off about. And for me, I was always in Tom‘s (my partner) ear about motherhood, and the challenges that modern mums have to face. From everything like being a working mum, and having to show up as a professional having a career, while being a mum, through to managing money stress, to feeling isolated geographically and emotionally from family. And so for a long time I was posting on my Instagram, but not really knowing what I was doing. Because I loved sharing about the reality of mum life, but I didn’t quite know how to actually help mums. I thought that just by being authentic, it was helping. Which I do think is one important part of it, but I also felt like social media used to leave me hanging with those relatable moments, but not actually giving me any tools to help.

This is why I created this Instagram account. I have such a passion for mums, and I just want mums to be able to enjoy those early years as much as they humanly can. Every child deserves a mum that is happy. 

I truly believe the world would be a better place if we all had happy mums. 

So here’s to empowering mums, or maybe better put, helping mothers reignite that power that they forgot they had along the way ❤️‍🔥

DYzMMBhjwEc.content:
I didn’t even know it, but motherhood was going to be THE thing that allowed me to find my innermost power. My most confidence. And my most strength. 

Of course, there are still hard days, where I feel like my confidence is shaky. 

But overall, I stand taller, I speak clearer, and with more certainty. And I know who I am. I know what I am about. I know what I value and what is important in my life. 

Motherhood gets to be your best era yet ❤️‍🔥

What a year 2025 was ! 
We started off pretty fresh going on holidays than it got shorty with our first miscarriage of the year that completely changed our life and our thoughts on extending our little family . 

We literally chased many many highs this year , going to more local outings ,
Chasing sunsets , enjoying each others company and trying to blend well as a family of 4 ! 

Riley had an extremely rough first semester then we started his ADHD management an started Ritalin . 

We started to see some personal wins and success in his learning over semester 2 and we couldn’t be prouder . 

We found out we were expecting another little bundle in may that turned our whole world back down side up ! 
Our little rainbow princess added hope and love to our family that we never thought we’d knew we needed and has allowed us to move onto our next chapter as a family of 5 ! 

We can’t wait to meet her in a few short weeks in February 🩷

Oliver Turned 2 ! 
He is such a ray of sunshine , full of fire and the biggest sweet heart ever ! 
He still however shy’a away around people and raids the boss aunty’s loll draw every time we leave school . 

He pushes the boundaries and tests limits , seeks curiosity, friendships and connections amongst others and is always full of surprises and new tricks . 

Let’s bring on 2026 , new adventures , thrill seeking and begin a new chapter as moving completely forward as a family of 5 ! 
We close the chapter of lots of last moments but will fill our lives with lots of firsts . 

Happy new year everyone 🥳 🥂 🎆

DVNT5o6D4Dg.content:
There’s a certain pride in our culture at bragging about non stop working. Superheroes push through and soldier on.

Under the cape, there’s a hidden cost for caregivers, healthcare workers and those in the helping industry: 

1️⃣ chronic stress = chronically living in survival mode, which over time brings generalized inflammation. I mean, look at my flared up SKIN in the picture ! Ouch.

This can also mean constant hypervigilance, alertness, bringing a string of other issues like digestive issues, insomnia. 

2️⃣ fragmenting, compartmentalization; not processing strong feelings, trauma, put it all in a box. Sorry to say this either festers, or comes out as trigger later. 
Let’s normalize de-briefing. Peer-support. Reflections or journaling. Somatic expression and release. And mental health Wellness. 

3️⃣ The Self-sacrificial worker is a victim of their belief about over-giving and constant productivity. No time for over flowing, receiving, rest, pleasure or joy. You may even start feeling guilty, a shadow of your former self, living on autopilot and dimming your light, slowly. 

“Your sensitivity is a compass, not a curse”
When we learn interoception we learn to tune inside our bodies, slowing repairing the numbness. Working with the breath and the nervous system, clients heal:

From Numbness -> To presence

Present. Radiant. Empowered. Breathing and Alive.

Very niche, very subtle, but wow very different experiences !

1. We assessed N’s functional breathing baseline and patterns. She realised she was shallow breathing, a dysfunctional technique and sign of stress. In one short session, her back and shoulder pain shifted.

DRhDG0YEoP9.content:
Most parents count down the days til their baby arrives, yet everyday we were praying you’d both stay in for another day longer.. 

We waited anxiously to be told you were “better out than in” and with every scan we watched that cord flow slowly go further and further backwards instead of forwards. 

Maternity leave started at 29 weeks, alongside a relocation 5 hours away from your dad, and our family. There was no nesting stage, no meals prepped for the freezer, no deep clean or organisation of the house.. Just a one-way trip to the city and a constant buzz of anxiety, hoping that you would both be okay. 

Your hospital bag was full of 00000 clothes that I knew would be far too big for either of you, my heart hurt that we wouldn’t get that iconic “I’m Here” picture for Instagram in cute, personalised onesies without there being a myriad of cords to navigate let alone the acrylic walls surrounding your tiny bodies. 

My blood pressure was inching higher as the days went on and my previously “normal” iron levels plummeted, resulting in admission to hospital, a concoction of beta blockers and an iron infusion to keep this machine ticking along.. cue the start of my sleepless nights with 4 hourly obs.

A panicked business owner (your amazing Daddy) frantically re-organised work, cleaned the house from top to toe, packed his bag and jumped on a flight to join me as we waited to be told you were both “better out than in”.

On Wednesday the 27th of November 2024, the wonderful Dr who had been looking after us all, told us we were going to meet you both within the hour.. We had made it to 33+1 weeks! We were reassured that you were both going to be just fine and that you can “fatten up” on the outside.

Everything from that point onward changed, I felt like I was watching it all play out from above, the disassociation was real. As they pulled you both out from my tummy, first Henley, then Oakley, I listened for those beautiful cries.. it was then I realised I had the most important job I’ll ever have, raising our sons 🩵🩵

#Firstyear #twinmum

DX5MzyJCZf6.content:
Hi there! Welcome, and thank you for being here 🤍

I’m Fanny, a certified babywearing educator based in Vaughan, ON.

Becoming a parent is a beautiful experience, but it can also come with challenges — and carrying your baby safely and comfortably can be one of them.

Whether you’re new to babywearing, unsure which carrier to choose, need help using it, or want to feel more confident in your technique, I’m here to support you.

Babywearing can fit so many moments of your daily life — at home, on the go, during walks or hikes, to soothe your baby, or simply to free your hands (because let’s be honest… we all need that).

Let’s find what works best for you and your baby 🍀

DYDwwAKkfpL.content:
🤍 Babywearing basics 

A few simple things to keep in mind when using a baby carrier (any carrier):

☁️ Knees above bum
Your baby’s legs should be in a spread squat position, with the knees higher than the bum, forming an “M” shape.

☁️ Natural back curve 
 A baby’s spine naturally forms a gentle curve. Their back should not be flat, but slightly rounded for comfort.

☁️ Airways clear 
Your baby’s airways should always be clear. Nothing should cover their face, and you should be able to see them at all times

☁️ Close enough to kiss. 
You should be able to kiss your baby’s head. A baby too low may lead to discomfort and back pain.

☁️ Don’t forget to actually kiss 
As much as you want ! Carrying your baby is a beautiful way to bond and stay close 🤍

Image credit : boba UK

DYS4QP2PwV1.content:
Babies are born with primitive reflexes that help them connect with and respond to the world around them.

The plantar grasp reflex — those tiny toes curling around a finger — is thought to be linked to babies’ instinct to cling to their caregiver, the same way baby apes cling to their mother’s fur. 

And even though humans have evolved beyond fur, it’s  a reminder that carrying isn’t ‘spoiling’, it’s how babies are wired.

#vaughanmoms #babywearing #vaughanmomlife #postpartumlove #babywearingeducator

DYcTML4OYSx.content:
Babywearing around the world — Episode 1

Among Inuit communities, babies are traditionally carried on their mother’s back during the first years of life. To keep both warm in Arctic conditions, mothers wear an Amauti — a parka designed specifically for Babywearing, with a built-in pouch in the back where the baby rests safely and close to the body.

Different places, same instinct for closeness 

Source : nanook of the North (1922)

A lot of people hear “FMLA” and immediately think it only applies to major medical emergencies or physical illness.

But the reality is: chronic stress, burnout, anxiety, panic attacks, and mental health conditions can become serious health issues too especially when they begin affecting your ability to work, function, sleep, focus, or care for yourself.

That’s why understanding your rights matters.

The Family and Medical Leave Act (FMLA) was created to protect employees who need time away from work for qualifying medical and family reasons. In many cases, mental health treatment, stress-related conditions, therapy programs, or burnout-related symptoms tied to a serious health condition may qualify for protected leave when certified by a healthcare provider.

Too many workers wait until they completely crash before asking questions about support or leave options.
Too many people feel guilt for needing rest.
Too many employees believe they have to “prove” they’re struggling enough to deserve help.

You do not have to earn rest by breaking down first.

Burnout is not just being tired. It can impact your nervous system, physical health, relationships, memory, concentration, and emotional well-being over time. Ignoring those warning signs doesn’t make them disappear; it usually makes recovery take longer.

Education is power. Understanding your workplace protections is part of protecting your health.

Rest is not weakness.
Support is not failure.
And using the resources available to you is not something to be ashamed of.

•During Pregnancy•
I’ve got all sorts of pregnancy symptoms (acid reflux throughout too), but the hardest was 3rd trimester where I have to deal with constant stabbing sciatica pain (do not miss that a single bit)

•Giving Birth•
It has to be the most excruciating pain I’ve ever felt going through natural birth. 😫
I did it with no pain relief because I didn’t know I was supposed to ask for it and the midwife was very motivating during birthing by making it seem like every push Eddie is almost out 😂 
Anyway it makes me question my mother why she thinks it’s a good idea to do this 4 times.😅
Thanks to this experience, I can never see mother the same ways anymore. 

•Recovery•
Due to the difficult birth, apart from tearing, my uterus was hanging out dangling like an upside down mountain 😩 (ya apparently it can happen, no kidding) 
Haemorrhoids hated me too 😆 swell to a thumb size from all that pushing.
I spend more than a month in laying position to eat and rest.
Honestly looking back it’s crazy how much and how hard my body have to work to recover even though I’m still not 100% yet.

•Parenthood•
As the saying goes, “It takes a village to raise a child.” I don’t exactly have a village nor my local food. So it’s been at times really hard and miserable. Dav always said, I have him in which I’m very thankful for. Nevertheless it’s different and very hard.

DAjXF2pSFaB.content:
My first book turns 2 years old today! 🐉🌊⚡️

I couldn't think of a better song for this book than this one. Kintsugi is the Japanese art of repairing broken pottery by mending the areas of breakage with urishi lacquer dusted or mixed with powdered gold, silver, or platinum. This actually reinforces the pottery and makes it stronger and more beautiful than ever. Kintsugi is seen as a metaphor for healing in grief and beauty in brokenness. 

So many times in my life I felt broken, beaten, and defeated by storms that came my way. But each time, God picked me up and put me back together, making me whole again, and more resilient for the next storm. His power is made perfect in my weakness. What others might see as flaws, He sees something beautiful. 

My main character, Shinju, definitely goes through the process of Kintsugi. She is crushed, but perseveres, and emerges stronger than she ever thought she could be. 

If you would like to read Shinju and the Master of Tides, it's available on Amazon and Barnes & Noble! Thank you all for an amazing two years with this book, I couldn't have done it without you!

Scorching heat. Terrifying monsters. Unpredictable weather. That is what awaits the contestants of the Namahea Desert Race. 

Every year, riders compete in a dangerous race with the finest horses in the kingdom to reach the finish line at the Capital City of Vestar. Winning would mean eternal glory. Losing could mean an agonizing death.

Growing up in Terah, the town that hosts the start of the Race in the southernmost province, Leyla Kamir looks forward to placing her bet on a rider. But when her merchant father is accused of illegal trading, their family's safety is in jeopardy until their debt to the crown is paid.

Then Leyla meets an Infernius, one of the legendary fire horses of the desert that haven't been seen for two hundred years. To her surprise, she does not burn at his touch, and a desperate plan to save her family is born.

As she enters the Race and faces the challenges of the desert, Leyla must determine friend from foe, and her actions ignite a chain of events that will change her life, and the kingdom, forever.

My reading and writing has been very sporadic since the beginning of 2025. I've had slumps where nothing sounded good, to rereading random childhood books, to speed reading YA athletic books on my kindle in the dark snatches of night between feedings. 

Becoming a mother is the greatest thing that's ever happened to me...and with it has come a different approach to reading. As my baby has gotten older it's been harder to read a physical book, easier to have the silent, one-handed kindle. I've started and DNF'ed so many books if they didn't snag my attention in the first couple of chapters. Or even the first few pages. I'm very selective and strict with what I'm going to spend my time invested in. 

I also fell into the screen time trap during naptime: scrolling or watching tv. I have a harder time focusing. My creative well has turned into a dry cistern with the barest trickle of water to keep it alive. 

But I'm finding renewed vigor. I'm longing to open the books on my TBR shelf you see in this reel. I'm longing to dive back into my writing and pour out the words that have been building up like a swell of water behind a dam. 

So slowly but surely I'm coming back. Learning to read again 🌸🫖

DXBxJnyEZXh.content: Yay for me!! First trail run race ever and first race post-partum. I love the atmosphere of an event way more than the training and it makes any training worthwhile. To be truthful, this had next to no training because I’ve been trying to juggle new mum life with exercise. Sometimes this looks like running with the pram in 36 degrees and others at 9pm when all I want is chocolate and bed. It’s included absolutely no trail running whatsoever so I had low expectations for this run and just wanted to have fun. In short: this was the hardest run course I’ve ever done in my life. The hill destroyed everyone, I could count on one hand how many people ran the entire way up the hill. But it was a beautiful course with river crossings, forest trails, bush bashing and good vibes. Could not get my HR below 198 and peaked it at 213! Need to go back to my heart doc - seems a bit wild. Anyhow, I got to 5.5km thinking I only had 500m left and went for a 5.40 pace which is fast for me. Little did I know the course was actually 7.1km and when I crossed the finish line I was practically hyperventilating and went and hid behind a bush to get myself together 🤣🤣🤣🤣 moral of the story, during the race I said this is dumb, after the race I’ve signed up for my next three in May and June. I had the support of Remy and Jesse at the finish line and could have cried seeing their faces 🫶 I am going to be sore tomorrow!!

Alas… Chase Atlantic slipped through my fingers again🙃 In a manic panic, I Googled the vinyl and every website took me to a 404 error page, SOLD OUT. Even with my @duolingo teachings, my ability to read in Japanese was not good enough to purchase a copy from Japan, ばか!!!!😡
A few hours later, a STRANGER remembers seeing my fb post more than a day ago. They send me a link that I hadn’t come across, BEHOLD- Resist Records still had copies!!!🤩 I managed to snag my new holy grail and for CHEAPER than advertised anywhere else, before thanking my saviour🎉 Side note: they picked a very questionable press “milky white” swipe to see and you’ve got one guess at what I’m calling it💦
This was the story of buying one of my favourite albums of all time, hope this took you on a journey🤪

CqKOun_PbQg.content:
Hallo! I'm Joanna of Coral Pea Designs. This business and my career as a watercolour artist is now a year old. This is my garden, where I have spent a lot of my time, between the pandemic and being bed & housebound for a year due to losing my muscles to Hyperemesis Gravidarum, a complication of my pregnancies. A lot of my paintings have been of plants photographed by my sister in law, Dr Laura Skates @floraskates, which helped me feel like my world was still connected when I was too weak to walk across a room. I am grateful that I can now share my joy of local plants with others through my painting.

If you want to learn more about what I do, you can ask in the comments, send me a DM for a chat or check out the link in my bio.

#HyperemesisGravidarum #SmallBusiness #WatercolourWesternAustralia

Not the tiredness. Something deeper than that. When the noise, the touching, the feeding, the broken sleep all stack up until your body simply cannot take in any more.

The most common thing people say to a new mum is “let me know if you need anything.”

And the most common thing a new mum does is never ask.

Not because she doesn’t need help. Because she’s too exhausted to figure out what to ask for, too proud to feel like a burden, or too deep in survival mode to even know what she needs.

So don’t wait to be asked.

Bring food. Real food, not snacks. Text “I’m dropping something at your door at 2pm” instead of “do you need anything?” Keep your visit to 30 minutes and only longer if the mum seems to be enjoying your company. Ask about her, not just the baby. Fold the laundry without asking. Load the dishwasher on your way out.

The mums who feel most supported aren’t the ones with the most visitors. They’re the ones whose people showed up without being asked.

Nobody warned me about the rage. Or the brain fog. Or the crying at literally everything.

Everyone knows about the nausea, the sore back, the fatigue. But there’s a whole side of pregnancy that barely gets mentioned, and it’s the part that catches most women off guard.

The rage that shows up out of nowhere. Not a bad mood. Actual fury, often directed at your partner, and you don’t even know why. That’s HCG and oestrogen, and it’s far more common than people admit.

The brain fog. Forgetting what you walked into the room for. Losing words. Feeling like you’ve lost ten IQ points. Your brain is actually pruning and rebuilding neural pathways to prepare you for motherhood. It’s not you going mad; it’s your brain reprioritising.

The sensory overload. Sounds are louder. Smells are unbearable. Being touched feels like too much. Your nervous system is becoming more alert, and sometimes it overshoots.

And the ones nobody talks about: intrusive thoughts about something terrible happening to your baby. Feeling disconnected from your bump when you expected to feel bonded. Quietly grieving the person you were before, even when you’re happy about the baby.

None of this means something is wrong with you. But it does mean you deserve more than a five-minute check-up that only asks about your blood pressure.

DWiFy0Tk3gp.content:
I did not experience this myself. But a client described it to me and it was the first time I had even heard of it. That surprised me.

You can be completely ready to stop breastfeeding and still feel like something is falling apart. And nobody tells you why.

Everyone talks about the baby blues. The overwhelming first few days after birth when your hormones crash and everything feels fragile. Most women expect that.

But almost no one mentions what can happen when breastfeeding ends.

I had not heard of this until someone described it to me. She had chosen to wean. She was ready. And then the sadness hit and she could not understand where it was coming from. That was the first time I looked into the weaning blues, and I was surprised that nobody was talking about it.

When you wean, your oxytocin and prolactin levels drop. These are the same hormones that have been regulating your mood, helping you bond, and keeping your nervous system steady for months. Sometimes years. When they fall, your body notices.

For some women it is a few days of feeling flat or teary. For others it is deeper. Irritability that comes out of nowhere. A grief you were not expecting. The confusing part is that the emotions do not match the decision. You wanted to stop. So why does it feel like loss?

That is not a sign you made the wrong decision. It is a hormonal shift, not an emotional failure.

I did not experience this myself. But I have seen how much it catches women off guard, especially when they have no idea it is even a thing. If you are planning to wean or in the middle of it, go gently and slowly with weaning. 

Rest more than you think you need to. And tell someone how you are feeling.

If this happened to you and nobody told you why, drop a comment. I think more women need to hear about this.

“It must be nice having so much time off.” 
Oh sure raising a baby and kids is like being on holiday 24/7 😒

Here is what is actually happening when a mum is “just” swinging with a baby on a swing. Rhythmic, predictable movement is one of the most powerful tools for infant nervous system regulation. It mimics the rocking she felt in the womb. It tells her brainstem: you are safe, you are held, the world is steady. This is co-regulation, and it is the foundation of secure attachment.

Add your face in her line of sight. Add the sound of your voice. Add the fact that every time she looks up, you are still there. That is the literal architecture of secure attachment being built in real time.

The first 1000 days of a baby’s life are when the brain decides what to expect from the world. Not from lessons or flashcards or developmental toys. From repetition. From the small, boring, beautiful moments exactly like this one. A swing. A hum. A mum who keeps showing up.

It is not maternity leave time off. It is the most foundational work a person can do. And the fact that nobody claps for it does not make it smaller. It makes it more important.

DXD7etTk8Su.content:
Postpartum exhaustion doesn’t just make you tired. It changes what your brain pays attention to.

When you’re running on broken sleep, your brain shifts into survival mode. It gets sharper at noticing stress, threats, and everything that feels hard. But the good moments? They start slipping through.

Not because they’re not happening. Because your brain doesn’t have the resources to hold onto them.

That moment on the swing. The way she laughed at the birds. Five minutes in the sun where nobody was crying. They happen. They just slide past before you register them.

Sleep deprivation amplifies your negativity bias. The hard stuff sticks. The soft stuff fades. You end up thinking nothing good happened, when it did.

Here’s what actually helps:

When something small feels good, pause for 10 seconds
Notice it. Name it out loud if you can. “This is a good moment.”
That pause is what your brain needs to encode it. Without it, it’s gone.

It won’t fix the 6 wake-ups. It won’t make the car ride quieter. But it changes what your brain holds onto at the end of the day.

DYvsXZxk1fr.content:
This one’s personal. It’s been a rough week.

Your brain needs about four hours of unbroken sleep to complete a full sleep cycle, the kind where memory consolidates, emotions process, and your nervous system actually recovers. When you’re waking every 90 minutes to feed, you’re not just getting “less sleep.” You’re getting almost no restorative sleep. Your brain never gets the chance to reset.

That’s why it doesn’t matter how many total hours you technically got. Broken sleep and short sleep are not the same thing as rest. Without those deep sleep stages, cortisol stays elevated, your amygdala (the part of your brain that detects threat) becomes hyperactive, and your prefrontal cortex, the part that helps you stay calm, think clearly, and regulate your emotions, can’t do its job properly.

So you snap. You feel guilty. You’re overwhelmed by mess. You flinch when your toddler touches you. You can’t enjoy anything. And then you tell yourself you’re a bad mum.

You’re not a bad mum. You’re a mum whose brain hasn’t had what it needs to function.

“Just 3 days and your baby will learn self soothing and independent sleep.” ✨🧚‍♀️

If you’ve been told by a baby sleep consultant that your baby can learn self-soothing in just days with a sleep training program - 
You BETTER continue reading 
⤵️

self-soothing develops over 
YEARS not days or weeks.

What science shows:

🧠 Babies are not born able to regulate stress
Their nervous system is still immature.

🤍 They rely on co-regulation first
Calm develops through repeated, responsive caregiving.

⏳ Regulation unfolds gradually
Through brain maturation, attachment, and safety - over months and years.

🧠 self soothing depends on brain systems that mature much later.
Including the prefrontal cortex, which supports emotional regulation.

Why the term “self soothing” is misleading:

⚠️ It suggests regulation can be taught quickly through a sleep training method.
⚠️ It creates unrealistic expectations for parents.

It works well for marketing.
But biology doesn’t work on promises.

If your baby still needs you to settle, soothe, or fall asleep…that’s not a failure of how your baby sleep.

#babysleep #selfsoothing #sleeptraining #sleepconsultant #babydevelopment

DT2O6SUCWss.content:
I never planned an unmedicated birth. 

Here’s what I learned while giving birth moment by moment:

1️⃣ Not having a birth plan was the BEST decision because it helped me stay flexible.
Education is important - I knew the options that might be offered to me.

Having a fixed plan would have anchored my brain to one outcome.
Birth is deeply mental, and flexibility mattered more than control.

2️⃣ I wouldn’t have known I could stand.
If my midwives hadn’t encouraged me to stand and move during contractions, I probably would’ve stayed on the bed a simply because that’s what we’re used to seeing.
Standing and moving actually helped me cope better with contractions.

3️⃣ Vocalisation became an unexpected coping tool
Moaning wasn’t embarrassing - it was regulation.
I felt animal, instinctive, like I dropped into another dimension.
Everything went quiet. I wasn’t “doing” birth anymore - I was inside it.

4️⃣ When I asked for the epidural she was literally minutes away.
The moment I panicked and screamed “I can’t do it” - I started losing my breating, my rhythm. 
But Breathing became everything.
I asked the midwives to speak right next to my ear because I couldn’t hear anything else. Their voices grounded me back into my body.

5️⃣ congratulations. You did it. please take a Quiet skin-to-skin. This matters more than anything
No phones. No questions. No visitors. Mot updating anyone. 
Skin-to-skin wasn’t just bonding - it’s allowing your nervous system settling, slowly returning back to life.

These aren’t universal birth tips.
Just one honest experience of an unmedicated birth, shared gently - in case it helps someone feel more informed, more prepared, or less scared. 🙌🏻

I’ll start with the uncomfortable truth:

There is currently no evidence showing developmental benefits of screen time in babies and toddlers.

None.

And there are enough studies suggesting that  screen exposure is associated with negative impacts on language, attention, and aspects of brain and emotional development.

Early brain development happens through:
🏃 Movement
🖐️ Sensory exploration
🤱🏼 Human interaction
🐣 Back-and-forth communication

Screens CANNOT replicate that.

***Now here’s the part nobody says out loud:

Postpartum is OVERWHELMING.

Parenting in a culture that expects you to work, earn, keep up with economic pressure, cook, clean, manage the mental load - and somehow stay regulated - is hard.

Sometimes you need 10 minutes to:
👉 cook dinner without the kitchen catching fire
👉 answer an urgent call
👉 breathe
👉 reset your nervous system

And in that moment, a screen can feel like the quickest solution.

I get it.

That doesn’t make you a bad parent.
It makes you human.

The real question is not:
“Have you ever used a screen?”

It’s:
“What is the pattern around it?”
“Is it occasional support - or constant replacement?”
“How much control do I have over it?”

Because your child’s brain is shaped by thousands of daily interactions.

These are the 5 psychology-based truths that protected my mental health while starting daycare:

1️⃣ Tears = Secure Attachment. (Ainsworth)
She protests because I am her safe haven. Securely attached children prefer their primary caregiver. Baby crying at separation isn’t damage - it’s connection.

2️⃣ Separation anxiety = A cognitive milestone. (Piaget)
Around 18-20 months, object permanence becomes stronger. She now understands I exist even when I’m out of sight. She is not regressing - she is developing.

3️⃣ The hug = The repair. (Tronick)
Attachment isn’t built on perfect goodbyes. It’s built on mismatch and repair. The reunion is what strengthens the bond.

4️⃣ Play = Progress. (Bowlby)
Success isn’t a tear-free morning. It’s exploration. She can be sad at the door and still activate her exploratory system once she feels safe.

5️⃣ My gut = My power. (Bandura)
Parental self-efficacy means I trust myself. If starting daycare ever stops feeling right, I can adjust the plan.

Starting daycare is hard.
But the science is clear:

Your bond is bigger than a heartbreaking baby crying at drop off. 🤍

This baby behaviour study at the University of Maryland by researcher Dr. Amy Hane observed two 9 month old babies.

🔬 Jack kept going back. Again and again. His mother had to work twice as hard just to keep up.

👉🏻 They didn’t raise their voice
👉🏻 They removed the plant
Because with a highly reactive baby -
the environment needs to adapt to them.
Not the other way around.

💡 If you have a Jack:
Before you repeat yourself again,
ask what you can remove from the room.
Not what you can say differently.

This isn’t a baby behaviour problem.
It’s a temperament difference.

DYhOw29pq08.content:
Giving birth is the moment I lost my old self. 
Here are 5 things I want you to know about that - from a postpartum perspective no one talks about. 👇

1. Your postpartum recovery journey won’t be linear. One day you’ll feel whole, one day you might feel completely broken. Both are part of the process. And it’s not 6 weeks! Postpartum recovery can take up to 2 years.

2. It’s okay to grieve your old self. Missing who you were before doesn’t mean you don’t love your baby. Or that you’re failing as a mother. Both can coexist. it is one of the most normal and least discussed experiences in early motherhood.

3. The worst advice anyone will give you after giving birth is “you’ll get back to yourself again.” Your body carried a human being. Your mind rebuilt itself around a new life. She isn’t lost. She EVOLVED. Looking for the old version will only keep you from meeting the new one.

4. What you are going through has a name and it’s called matrescence - the neurological, hormonal and psychological transformation a woman goes through when she becomes a mother. Your brain literally rewires itself. It was identified in 1973 and we still barely talk about it.

5. When someone asks “how can I help?” and you go blank that’s not you being difficult. Your nervous system is in survival mode. Your mental load is at capacity. You are not supposed to have the answer. The people around you are supposed to show up anyway.

Giving birth will change you life.
Postpartum is not a phase to push through. Share it with a postpartum mum who needs it🤍

#givingbirth #realmotherhood #mothersday #postpartum #newmum

DYj1m5WibO6.content:
No one prepared you for the baby sleep advice that was coming.

From the moment a mother gives birth - before anyone asks about her postpartum recovery - she will be asked: “how is the baby sleeping?” “Are they sleeping through the night yet?”

Sleep train. Don’t sleep train. Bad habits. Wake windows. And somehow through all of it, you are left wondering what you did wrong.

Nothing. You did nothing wrong.

The research on baby sleep tells a very different story to what most parents are handed. Studies consistently show that night waking is statistically normal well beyond the first year. How easily a baby self-settles is largely temperament, NOT a result of your choices.

If your baby is not sleeping through the night, that is not evidence of failure. It is evidence of a developing nervous system doing exactly what it is supposed to do.

The baby sleep industry is worth billions. Your sleep deprivationhas been turned into a product. In a world of completely unregulated sleep advice, the most radical thing you can do is trust the baby sleeps research over the noise.

Your baby’s sleep is not a measure of your worth as a mother.

DFp5k4sIzNH.content:
Let's talk about our surroundings! 

When I first started nannying, I didn't really know what to do while we were waiting for a bus to go somewhere. I was used to nurseries where there were always activities on offer and resources that could be fetched with ease, and floundered for ways to entertain the small child I was looking after. I'd sing, offer paper and pens to draw and colour, we'd play imagination games with any toys we happened to have on us, but all those got old quite quickly and I found myself at a loss.

But then I realised there's an infinite source of things to do at the bus stop! We could watch the cars go past and name their colours, look at the map at the bus stop and see where we were then trace it to where we were going, even practice climbing and balancing on the bench (if no one was sitting there)!

It was surprising how many insightful and engaging conversations could spring from a random occurrence like someone running for the bus or seeing a lorry deliver wares to a nearby shop. Letting the child take the lead, I found myself asking questions I'd never have thought of otherwise, like "What kind of stone are paving stones made from?" and "How does the bus lean over to make it easier for passengers to get on?".

And from these conversations new interests formed - one child became enamored with "second decker" buses and so we planned special outings making sure we could take a double decker. We found difficulty in taking the collapsible buggy up the stairs, so we made a new plan to walk to the bus stop without the buggy and celebrated our mutual resilience and problem solving abilities. He started insisting we didn't take the buggy on every outing and accepted that he would have to carry his "packpack", learning responsibility, spacial awareness, and improving his physical endurance and awareness of time in relation to our walking speed. 

All that from a stray thought at a bus stop.

DGGiuqkI2UV.content:
When I was 19, I briefly worked in a nursery in Thornton Heath. It's not there anymore, but that's a story for a different time. I was working in the preschool room and got the children ready to go out to the garden attached to the building.

When I realised I'd misread the time and it wasn't our turn yet I apologised to the children for getting them excited and told them I'd read them a story after they went and put their coats and shoes back. While they did that my room leader pulled me aside and quietly told me not to apologise to children, because it made adults look bad and the children had to believe adults were to be obeyed without question. She didn't phrase it exactly like that, but that was the general gist.

Now that just didn't sit right with me. I remembered being a child and noticing when adults floundered and fell back on "because I said so". It made me respect them less, not more. So while I was too young and anxious to contradict her at the time I made a silent decision to always apologise to a child when I made a mistake.

Nearly 10 years later I can now confidently say I made the right decision. In every nursery I worked in after that, and afterwards when I started nannying, I made a point to admit and apologise to the children in my care if I made a mistake. They quickly realised I'd treat them fairly if they did the same, and many children confided in me things they wouldn't tell coworkers who were (let's be polite here) slightly more high strung. 

This decision also changed how I interacted with adults during and outside of work - not just coworkers but friends, family, and loved ones. A lot of issues that could have become arguments instead became discussions about our values and boundaries. Things that could have become deep seated resentment instead became opportunities to explain our viewpoints and be vulnerable with each other. It strengthened my relationships and reinforced people's trust in me because they knew I'd admit when I was wrong instead of refusing to engage. 

So thank you to that room leader. You were wrong, but you provided me with an opportunity to be better as a friend, a partner, and a caregiver.

DHoZuR7I69i.content:
Trauma is weird. I've made so much progress in the last 10 years, and the last ~5 years especially, mostly due to being surrounded by a network of friends and partners willing to give love and support at the drop of a hat. Also therapy. A lot of therapy.

Today was a good day, objectively. It started off stressful but I managed not to let that set my mood for the day, which anyone who knows me can tell you is a big step forward. I did well at work, made friends with a parent at the school, my current kid is improving his schoolwork and his emotional skills. I even took an uber home even though I didn't "need" to - just last year I would have forced myself to walk because I couldn't afford or didn't deserve such a luxury.

Yet I feel nauseous with guilt right now. Why? Because as a child I was conditioned to be wary of feeling good. The mood of the household depended on the mood of my parent, and at any point laughter could turn into guilty silence after an outburst of anger. I learned to be quiet and walk on eggshells. I'm ashamed to admit I tried to blame my brothers sometimes, because I was so scared of having that anger directed at me.

Winter was the worst, because those grey days meant their Seasonal Affective Disorder was in full swing. Extra sharp mood swings could be triggered by something that was fine yesterday and would be fine again tomorrow. The fact they were likely struggling with depression and anxiety themselves doesn't change the fact that that emotional instability (and the coping mechanisms I developed in response) became carved into my bones. I still can't deal with gloomy rooms and need to have the "big light" on to feel safe in my own home.

How we as adults act around children shapes the rest of their life. Using your child as an emotional stress toy leaves scars, even if you didn't mean to do it. I'll likely never get an apology, seeing as last time I tried to talk to them about it they told me "I'm sorry you chose to be upset by what I said". I'm almost OK with that now. And it feels better knowing I'm doing what I can to make sure the children in my care don't develop scars of their own.

I've recently started teaching myself embroidery, and it's made me think about how a few years ago, my then-3 year old NK ripped a hole in his favourite pyjamas. He was very upset at the idea of throwing them out because he's very particular about his clothes and forms strong attachments to personal items, so his mum messaged me asking if I was any good at sewing.

I said I would do my best, and came over the next morning armed with a brand new travel size sewing kit. Once NK understood I was going to fix his pyjamas he was delighted and wanted to be involved in every step of the process. I gave him the very important jobs of choosing the colour of thread I used, and making sure his baby brother didn't touch any of the sharp pins — both of which he took Very Seriously. He watched in fascination as I threaded the needle and pinned the sides of the rip together, and once it was done he pored over it before telling me "You did a good job, Elliott," which was the highest praise he could think of 😂

After that he'd ask every now and then to see my sewing kit, and informed me each time that "[baby brother] can't touch these [the pins] because they're sharp". It was so lovely to see his happiness over the pyjamas and to know how much he cared about his brother's safety. I still have that little sewing kit in my rucksack - I used it recently to sew up a rip in a well-loved octopus teddy for another former NK, and now I'm using it to fix my hat. Even though I don't see any of those children regularly anymore, the memories associated with them will stay with me long after I've used up all the thread it contains.

Nannying jobs are transient by their nature - children grow up, families move away, new opportunities present themselves. But I'll always have that feeling of pride in "my" kids' growth as people, and that's what really matters.

DPSB0cmCMHk.content:
Today was a really good day. Signore (almost 5yo nanny kid) is autistic and mostly nonverbal, and I'm still learning to interpret his scripts and vocalisations. I've let my own anxieties about being viewed as a competent care provider bleed into our interactions in the past and after a big meltdown last week I was scared I'd tainted his view of me.

But today, for the first time ever, he actively sought me out to ask me to play with him. Usually he'll respond positively to my additions to his solo play or ignore me entirely. He came to me across the playground and said "help me". He took my hand and led me to the play structure, climbed up the steps and stopped at a corner where there's a fire pole and a slide. I assumed he wanted me to hold him while he went down the fire pole, which is something we've done before, but when I stood under the gap in the play structure he gestured and said "up up". When I climbed up he pulled me to sit down behind him then arranged our bodies so my legs were either side of his body facing the slide. We went down the slide together and I felt like my heart was going to burst with happiness. 

It just goes to show that humans can be incredibly forgiving, and that consistently showing people you're there to help and comfort and support is more important than the mistakes you've made in the past. 

It can be difficult to see the positive when you grow up in an environment where mistakes are brought up over and over. That doesn't mean you have to do the same thing for the rest of your life. You can forgive yourself, and other people will forgive you too. On the bus home he started falling asleep, and when we got off he indicated that he wanted me to carry him. That's very new too; he's very sensitive to touch, and doesn't often permit me to do more than pass a hand through his hair or tickle him a little. I feel privileged he trusts he to carry him home. And yes, my back aches and I think I pulled something in my side. But I'd do it every day if that's what I need to do to make sure he knows I'm there for him.

DQZF1aTCF2H.content:
Yesterday was a win in my personal/professional improvement project.

I've been making a conscious effort to let go of what others might think and focus solely on the child. It seems basic when I lay it out like that, but I've noticed that I stress a lot about what should be happening—and what counts as acceptable—in my work. But it's often an amorphous blend of past coworkers, parents, things said online, and the concept of people on the street deciding what should be and what's acceptable. Those hypothetical people aren't in my care, they're not professionals, and they're not paying me. They're just weird blobs in my brain trying to make me feel bad and That's Not On.

So when I picked up Signore from his house it was with the plan to go to the playground nearby. There are four different structured places for children to play - a big playground, a little playground, a trim trail type deal, and a larger standalone climbing frame. But when we got to the playground he took off like a mad thing past all of those and headed straight for the low wooden fence that surrounds the carpark.

At first I tried to herd him back to the playgrounds. I offered snacks, juice, even my umbrella (and nearly got my eye punctured for my effort) but he didn't want any of it. He just wanted me to help him balance on the fence. And I realised, why not? Why shouldn't I accept his offer to play, just because it's different to what I imagined? Why shouldn't I hold his hands, help him practice balance and proprioception, catch him when he falls, pretend he's an aeroplane as I carry him across the gaps he's too small to jump? Because someone might judge us for it? Screw that. He's going to be five next month. He'll never be four again, and I'm not going to let his last month of being four be anything less than the fullest it can be.

So we did that for half an hour, and yeah my arms ached but I got to spend time with a kid I adore. We got to be happy and have fun without worrying what strangers might think. We played the way he wanted instead of how we were "supposed to" play, and no one died. It was good. I love my job.

#nanny #NannyLife #FreedomToBe #autism #ASD #AutisticAdult

Or I could use it to be better next time.

And next time—Wednesday—was better. I made the conscious decision to let go of my preconceived idea of What We're Doing Today. I let him take the lead and only gently nudged him towards the bus stop so by the time he got tired, we were almost there already. We had a picnic, he rode on my shoulders and giggled when I kissed his knees, we chased birds and narrowly avoided disrupting a football game. When we got home he was tired, but not in meltdown territory.

Friday I had to cancel last minute because my sleep schedule was so badly screwed up I was totally brain fogged, and it wouldn't have been safe for me to look after him. It's embarrassing and frustrating to feel like I'm ruled by my disability on days like that, but I'm extremely grateful I have clients who understand and accept my limits. Still working on doing that for myself.

Saturday I had my first 10 hour shift since I started self employment, babysitting an extremely sweet 13mo. It was certainly a lot less stressful to have just one child instead of up to 12 to look after, as is common in nursery work. Even looking after the family dog alongside the baby didn't cause a noticeable increase in difficulty. Baby was not a fan of the heavy metal nursery rhymes I put on (although apparently headbanging is hilarious) so we swapped to generic nursery rhymes and had a dance party after nap time. We hung out in the garden with the dog for a while, and back inside we played "how many dangerous things can I find before Elliott puts them out of my reach?". It's a worldwide game for a reason I guess.

Overall I give last week a "you can do this" out of 10.

DSU5HjbiGr8.content:
I've been thinking a lot about community lately, and gratitude, and how the things we do include quiet affirmations of care whether we know it or not.

A friend asking me if one of my work kids needs a rain jacket isn't just an attempt to be rid of that jacket. It's a way of saying I love you and I care about the people you care about even if we've never met.

One of my partners chopping the veg and putting everything in pans so all I have to do to make dinner is turn on the hob isn't just giving me a hand with dinner. It's saying I noticed you're tired, and even though I'm tired too I'll use what energy I have to make your life easier. 

My other partner listing the people at a party where I'm not familiar with everyone isn't just helping me to match names to faces. It's saying I know you struggle with faces, and I know you're trying to remember my friends because you care about me, so I'll help you because I care about you too. 

The postie calling out to me on the street to give me a package isn't just doing his job. He's saying I know you, I care about you enough to personally hand you your package when I could have just left it on the doorstep, because you care about me as a human being enough to stop and chat on the street. 

My nanny kid's mum offering me food, checking I'm OK isn't just being a good host. She's saying you're a part of my life, my son's life, and I care about your wellbeing. 

This isn't just a painted rock. It's a symbol of love and care from children I only see every few months, but who think about me when I'm not there as much as I think about them. It's a display of affection from their parents, who could just pay me for the job I'm doing and leave it at that. But they took the time to help their children make this, made the effort to gloss it so the paint doesn't flake off, to give me a physical reminder of the community I've built in the past few years I've lived here.

And from me to the handful of people who read these posts - whether you celebrate Christmas, any other winter holiday, or you're just taking the time to slow down and relax, I hope you get what you want this year.

DTmMUWdAWCB.content:
Many women fear bread and butter (in my 20’s I did too) but traditionally, these were staples so nourishing that butter was often given to boost fertility and support pregnancy.

The problem isn’t the foods, but what modern processing and dietary trends have done to them. 

In the 70’s & 80’s saturated fat and cholesterol were blamed for disease. Butter was replaced with margarine, bread lost its fermentation and low-fat, high-sugar foods flooded the market. Later, carb-free diets like Atkin’s added more food fear.

But In reality these staple foods are a nutritious part of a well rounded diet.

Sourdough bread does not spike blood sugar, it’s easily digested & nutrient rich, while butter provides vitamins A, D, E, K2, omega-3s, CLA, butyrate, and cholesterol, all essential for hormones, reproductive health, and fetal development. 

These staple foods don’t need to be feared, butter especially is a nutrient dense super fertility food.

It’s the processed fats and extreme diets are what I wish more women would question. 

We have a lot to learn by looking back 🤍

DVVekhVEoeU.content:
If only every girl was taught this growing up, I truly believe we wouldn’t see the level of fertility confusion and complications we’re seeing.

Here’s how to start understanding ovulation:

1️⃣ Pay attention when you go to the bathroom.

As you walk there, what do you SENSE at your vulva? Dry? Damp? Wet? Slippery? 

Your vulva is highly sensitive, when you tune in you will be able to feel changes.

Then check what you SEE when you pull your underwear down. Is there cervical mucus? Dry? Tacky? Creamy? Stretchy? Slippery? This is showing you real-time info about your hormones.

As oestrogen rises as you near ovulation, mucus becomes more watery that’s what we’re tracking. Each day, write down the most fertile sign you notice.

2️⃣ Don’t count days and assume you know when you ovulate.

Every woman’s fertile window is different. Not everyone ovulates on day 14. Even with a 28-day cycle, ovulation could be day 11… or day 16. Charting your signs gives clarity on YOUR unique window. 

NOTE: The rhythm method is inaccurate because it ignores stress, illness, travel, sleep — this is where most apps fail. I do not teach the rhythm method.

3️⃣ Look for patterns.

After a few months, your data will show you your unique fertile and non fertile windows. This is how we time intercourse accurately…. not by guessing, but through informed body literacy.

🌷🌷🌷🌷

To be a woman is to hold so many roles at once…. mother, daughter, sister, friend, partner, caregiver, creator, leader. To follow passions, build careers, nurture families, hold space for others, and still keep discovering who we are along the way.

Women carry so much. We create life, grow life, nurture life…. and we also build businesses, lead communities, chase dreams, and shape the world around us. 

I’m so grateful for the community of women around me. For the ones who lift each other up instead of competing. Who celebrate each other’s wins, hold space through hard moments, there for the big laughs and the big cry’s. A community of loving, supportive women can have the most profound ripple effect. 

But one of the greatest privileges of my life is raising a little girl, to know her worth, her strength and softness, courage and empathy and to raise her knowing that anything is possible. 

Happy International Women’s Day 🤍

DWGRYxxiFeu.content:
Trust me when I say this comes from a woman who used to not know how to slow down. It took deep practice.

We’re living in a world full of hurried women. And it goes against our biology. The pressure to do more, be more is impacting you more than you may realise. 

It chips away at your mental health, your sense of happiness, and your hormonal health and fertility.

Because from a biochemical perspective, constantly being “on” keeps your body in a fight-or-flight state. You’re pumping out stress hormones like cortisol and adrenaline, which can disrupt ovulation, hormone balance, and even your ability to sustain a pregnancy over time.

This is why I speak so much about becoming an unhurried woman.

And please don’t eye roll and think that Slowing down means you can’t be ambitious.

It doesn’t mean you stop doing all the incredible things you’re here to do.

It means living in alignment with your biology.
It means creating moments in your day to pause, to breathe, to check in.
It means having the tools to regulate your nervous system when you feel yourself tipping into overwhelm.

Your body is always giving you feedback, it will let you know when you feel nourished and in balance, and when you’re feeling a little off and need more care. It’s your job to listen.

🤍

DWTL1GdCLGa.content:
Working in the fertility space, I so often sit with women who’ve been on contraception for 10–20 years… and when they come off it, they feel completely disconnected from their bodies.

They don’t know their signs of fertility or when they’re ovulating.

They feel like they’ve been left in the dark.

And it really makes me question the narrative we’ve been fed as women…. that shutting down ovulation for years is the “easier” path.

This isn’t to say contraception doesn’t have its place, it absolutely does.
But somewhere along the way, we stopped teaching women how to understand their bodies in the first place.

Because your cycle isn’t just about getting pregnant.
Ovulation is a marker of health and it can tell us so much about what’s happening in the body.

This is something I’ll be teaching inside Journey to Motherhood - how to deeply understand your body’s signs across the month, so you can confidently identify ovulation and know when the time is right to conceive.

Because when you understand your body, you’re no longer guessing, you’re working with it.

And we have research to show that identifying your fertile window can significantly reduce the time it takes to conceive.

This is the kind of education I believe every woman deserves to learn 🤍

If you’d like to learn more DM me CYCLE

DWgB3Y3iNFX.content:
When you really stop and think about what’s happening in those first few weeks of pregnancy… it’s absolutely mind-blowing.

Before most women even know they’re pregnant, the foundations are already being laid… from the baby’s genetic blueprint, to the early development of the brain and spine, to the beginnings of the placenta. And all of this is shaped by the nutrients and environment before conception even occurs.

This is why I am so passionate about preconception care. 
Doing the work before conception is not just about getting pregnant (yes that is a big part of it) but it’s also about ensuring you have a health pregnancy, and the start to your future baby’s life is as good as it can be.

DMk_uIzNwcZ.content:
The bog is the oldest organic landscape in Estonia, reaching in some cases up to 10 000 years of age. At the very beginning, this peat accumulation landscape does not have a significant effect on plants. After millennia or two, the peat layer becomes thicker and filters out more demanding plants. The last stage is called a bog or raised bog. Here you can see a lot of bog pools or lakes inside this huge organic sponge. The water in the bogs is acidic because of the sphagnum moss.
Water is really pure and drinkable, but won't take your thirst away (remember, no minerals/nutrients!). That's how @visitestonia introduced the bogs. Allow me to add, they are one of my favorite choices for swimming.

Undervalued*
I only realised how unequal we still are after becoming a mom. Our work is tremendously valuable. Raising a human is the most difficult yet most rewarding job, but the patriarchal system decided otherwise. In Canada, you get one year of mat leave paid 70% of your salary the first six months and 55% the last six months. In the US you get 12 weeks and in Brussels it’s about the same. Mothers told me they were threatened to loose their job if they took longer mat leaves. We need men to advocate for us as well. We are mothers, we are creators of life. We hold superpowers. 

#momlifeunfiltered #womensupportingwomen #internationalwomensday #firsttimemom expatmom

DW8ocrtCMxC.content:
Ever since giving birth and moving to a new country, my nervous system has felt constantly overstimulated. Lately, the stress of job searching has made me feel stuck and blocked in so many ways. A friend recently told me that she went for a drive to clear her head on a bad day, but realized that walking made her feel even better. It reminded me why movement is such a powerful way to regulate our nervous system. We see this so clearly in children, yet we often forget that the same principle applies to adults.

When we spend too much time in our heads, we disconnect from our bodies. The simplest way to reconnect is to move — to remind our mind that we have a body, and to rebalance our energy through that awareness. Today, after feeling discouraged about putting effort into job hunting without seeing results, I got up and danced to a song that resonated with how I felt in that moment. You can tell I have blockages in the way I move. My hips ache, my pelvic floor still hasn’t fully recovered, and although I used to dance and work out regularly, I haven’t moved my hips in a long time. But it still felt good — really good. This is your reminder to move your body, in any way, any form that speaks to you, to release energy that is stuck. 

#NervousSystemHealing
#MindBodyConnection
#PostpartumJourney
#MoveToHeal

DYH2u1nCE3R.content:
My birth story 🤍

Pregnancy was nothing like I imagined. The first 4 months, I was sick all day, every day. I could barely get out of bed, and sometimes my legs would tremble so much I’d fall trying to stand. I got pregnant while living in the Dolomites, in a tiny village in Italy called Agordo, far away from family and support, with only my husband by my side.

Eventually, we made the difficult decision for me to move back to Montreal to stay with my mom while my husband moved to Turin for work. My mom took such good care of me, and I’ll always be grateful for her. During pregnancy, I became anemic, struggled with very low blood pressure, and had to call an ambulance twice after nearly fainting. I thought I’d stay active throughout pregnancy, but even workouts made me dangerously dizzy.

My husband came back two weeks before my due date, and I was induced so he could be there for the birth. On December 11 I had a stripping and on December 12, contractions started at 4am. The pain was immediate and intense. By the time we drove to the hospital, I felt like I couldn’t survive the ride. I asked for the epidural the second I walked in 😅

I dilated incredibly fast to 9cm… but then came the hardest part. I pushed for 4–5 hours. The epidural only worked on one side of my body, and I was close to an emergency C-section. Then my doctor looked at me and said: “Sabine, your baby is in critical condition. You have to push hard now. You can do it.”

And somehow, I did. 17 hours later.

I’ll never forget her encouragement in that moment. My baby was finally here 🤍 I only held her for a few seconds before they had to rush her away for oxygen for the next 5 hours. Having her taken from me broke my heart. A few hours later, I asked the nurses to wheel me to her. She was crying in her incubator, and all I wanted was to hold my baby.

The hardest and most beautiful day of my life.
