DYUrKV9jNeP.content:
Let’s set the record straight...Breast milk doesn’t magically stop being protective at 6 months! 🤪

It adapts. It strengthens. It intensifies.

🦠 Immune protection?
Breast milk contains live leukocytes - immune cells that increase in concentration when baby or mother is sick. These cells don’t vanish after infancy. They rise when they’re needed most.
(Riskin et al., 2012)

🧠 Brain development?
Breast milk provides DHA and other critical fatty acids long into early childhood - when the brain is still wiring itself at lightning speed.
By age 5, the brain is 90% of its adult size.
(Dewey, 2001; Victora et al., 2016)

🦷 Jaw, teeth, and airway health?
The act of breastfeeding promotes healthy jaw growth, proper tongue function, and better alignment of the palate and teeth.
It reduces the risk of malocclusion and future orthodontic issues.
(Peres et al., 2015; Viggiano et al., 2004)

💗 Emotional regulation and resilience?
Breastfeeding supports co-regulation, lowers cortisol, and fosters secure attachment - especially in highly sensitive or neurodivergent children.
(Jansen et al., 2008)

🌱 Independence?
Children who are allowed to self-wean on their own timeline often become more independent, not less.
Because when safety is internalised, confidence grows.
(Dettwyler, 2004)

So no - the benefits of breastfeeding don’t “tail off.”
They evolve.
They deepen.
They rise to meet the child - and the moment.

The only thing that wanes with time?
The public’s tolerance for breastfeeding beyond infancy.

And that says more about society than it does about science.

How long does it take for your period to return after birth? 
Can you get pregnant whilst breastfeeding? 
Why hasn’t my period come back postpartum?

These are some of the most searched questions in early motherhood. And they are some of the most common ones in my inbox too. So what's the answer? 

Breastfeeding suppresses ovulation through prolactin and its effect on the HPO axis (the hormone loop that runs your cycle). But the timeline of your period returning varies enormously from woman to woman and the science still has HUGE gaps in it.

I think those gaps are grossly unfair. We deserve clear answers about our own bodies. But where the data falls short, we can still use what we do have to inform us, to steady us and to make decisions from a place of knowledge rather than fear:

DYhaUQwANGL.content:
Last week, a major publication, @theeconomist, told millions of women that their bodies might simply be unable to feed their babies. The figure they leaned on: 10 to 15%, sounded authoritative. Final. Scientific.

So I went and read the research (again) for myself. Had there been another pivotal study published since I had done the research for myself own book? 

That number isn’t wrong, exactly, but it isn’t true in the way it’s being presented either. It appears in review papers as something “believed” or “estimated” - and when you trace it back, it doesn’t lead to a single robust study of the wider population. Not one. It leads to a figure that’s been repeated so often it began to sound like fact.

Underneath it all are three very different truths that have been conflated and folded into one: 
women who perceive low supply
women with a low measurement taken in small self-selected studies
and women with genuine, biological primary insufficiency. 

Those are not the same group. Treating them as one inflates the fear and blurs the facts.

I want to be really clear about something, because it matters: primary lactation insufficiency is real. Some women genuinely cannot produce a full supply and they deserve proper diagnoses, real clinical support and zero judgement. I will always hold space for every one 🙏🏽

But most of the women reading this? Your struggles in those early weeks were far more likely about support, information and a rocky start, not an underlying biological/physiological issue. 

This is what I want this little corner of the internet to be. A place where we don’t accept fear dressed up as fact. Where we ask who a headline serves before we let it live in our heads? Where mothers are trusted with the full picture, caveats and all - not simply handed a verdict.

You were never the problem, mama. But the narrative you were given was.

If this reframed something for you, send it to a mother who needs to read it today. Because empowerment comes from facts + support, not scaremongering headlines.

DYkaz3UjewY.accessibility_caption:
Slide 1:
“How can I increase my milk supply?” Perhaps the most FAQ in breastfeeding history.

Slide 2:
I’d like to start by recognizing that low supply issues are real, not imagined, and for some mothers, like those with Insufficient Glandular Tissue (IGT), no amount of hydration, supplements or pumping will change that.

Slide 3:
There is also a difference between having low supply and no supply at all. Breastfeeding doesn’t have to be all or nothing. Every. Single. Drop. Counts. Colostrum alone contains millions of immune cells per drop, and mature milk dynamically increases its immune content when you or baby are unwell.

Slide 4:
The reality is that anywhere between 0.1% and 5% of mothers will not be able to produce breast milk at all. Anecdotally, it is estimated that 10 to 15% of mothers may not be able to breastfeed exclusively due to true low supply. The data here is unclear.

Slide 5:
So if you have a true low supply and you want to produce as much milk as your unique body will allow, what can you practically do?

Slide 6:
Perhaps the simplest and most effective method? Allow your baby to use you like a pacifier or dummy. They’re not actually using you, and you’re not a dummy — breasts are nature’s original pacifier.

Slide 7:
The idea that comfort-nursing doesn’t count is a myth. Milk supply is driven by frequency of suckling and breast emptying — the more often a baby is at the breast, the more prolactin is released and the more milk is produced.

Slide 8:
Babies who comfort-nurse are still stimulating your milk supply. In fact, sucking pressure during non-nutritive sucking, when no milk is necessarily flowing at the breast, has been measured as higher than during active milk transfer.

Slide 9:
Comfort nursing 10 or more times in a 24 hour period will not necessarily ensure that every mother who wants to can exclusively breastfeed, but it will support mothers to produce as much milk as is possible for them and their body, in their circumstances.

Slide 10:
I share all of this with a potent reminder that a deep, comfortable, effective latch is vital for removing milk from your breasts. The best way for you and your baby to achieve this is with in-person support from an IBCLC.

Slide 11:
Adapted from my Penguin debut, The Breastfeeding Survival Guide by Danielle Facey.

Folate: The Key to Fertility & a Healthy Pregnancy 🌱
When it comes to fertility and pregnancy, folate (vitamin B9) is essential for both mom and baby! It plays a critical role in DNA synthesis, cell division, and most importantly, the formation of the spinal cord and neural tube—key areas of early fetal development. Adequate folate intake helps prevent birth defects like spina bifida and supports healthy fetal growth.

However, not all folate is created equal! 🌿 Methylated folate and folinic acid are the most bioavailable forms of folate, meaning they are easily absorbed and utilized by your body. In contrast, folic acid (the synthetic form) can be harder for some people to metabolize and has been shown to be less effective, potentially even detrimental during pregnancy. Opt for methylated folate or folinic acid in your supplement for optimal support in your fertility and pregnancy journey! 💚

Additionally, natural forms of folate can be found in foods such as: 
- Eggs
- mangoes
- Beetroot 
- Avocados
- Leafy greens like spinach kale broccoli
- Beans chickpeas and edamame
- Lentils 
- Pawpaw (papaya)
- Bananas

- Nuts: almonds, pistachios, walnuts & cashews
- Seeds: sunflower, sesame, flax, chia, pumpkin

DDoIIZyyjev.content:
This post deserves 2 days worth of Christmas, because there is nothing worse than family members or friends you are catching up with who have no idea of the journey you have been going through, asking intrusive and insensitive questions like “so when are you having kids?” “When are you going to give us another baby?” “When am I having grandkids?”

Setting clear and respectful boundaries is a healthy way to protect yours and your partners emotional well-being.

1.Set expectations early on- Even if it’s a group or individual text message to someone you know would ask.  “Before we talk about anything, I just want to mention that we’re not in a place to discuss the topic of our fertility (struggles). I hope you can respect that.”

2. Direct but gentle response “I appreciate your concern, but we’d prefer not to talk about our fertility journey right now. It’s something we’re working through privately.”

3. Change the subject “I know you mean well, but I’m not ready to discuss that. Let’s talk about something else—how have you been doing lately?”

4. Express need for privacy “We’ve decided to keep our fertility journey private for now. It’s a personal topic for us, and we’d appreciate your understanding.”

5. Be honest about your emotional state “That’s something that’s been really tough for us, and talking about it can be difficult right now. I hope you understand.”

6. Redirect the question “We’re still figuring things out, but I’d love to hear what’s new with you! Any exciting news on your end?”

Tips for Maintaining Boundaries:
* Be Consistent: You may have to gently repeat yourself a few times. People often forget or don’t realize how uncomfortable their questions can be.
* Stay Calm: It’s okay to feel frustrated, but try to keep a calm tone to avoid conflict. You have every right to protect your privacy.
* Know When to Step Back: If someone is pushing you repeatedly or not respecting your boundaries, it may be necessary to limit or pause communication for a while to protect your mental health.
It’s completely okay to set these boundaries, and doing so can help you maintain emotional and mental well-being during such a sensitive time

🔥 Cortisol Spike = Fat Storage Waking up = naturally high cortisol. Drinking coffee first thing raises it even more, signaling your body to hold onto weight, especially around the belly!
🌺 Cortisol spike plus hormonal roller coaster: 
Caffeine can interfere with estrogen and progesterone balance, potentially affecting ovulation and implantation. It also constricts blood vessels, reducing blood flow to the uterus. High caffeine intake has been linked to an increased risk of early pregnancy loss. In men, excessive caffeine may lower sperm count, reduce motility, and cause DNA fragmentation, impacting overall sperm quality.
⚡ Blood Sugar Rollercoaster Coffee alone = temporary energy boost → crash → cravings 😵‍💫. This leads to mood swings, brain fog, and insulin resistance over time.
🧠 Nervous System Chaos No food = increased anxiety, jitters, & stress response. Protein first helps keep your brain & body calm and focused.
✅ The Fix: Protein Before Coffee Start your day with:
🥚 Protein (eggs, Greek yogurt, lean meats) 🥑 Healthy fats (avocado, nuts, olive oil) 🥗 Fiber (veggies, whole grains) 👉 THEN, enjoy your coffee! ☕💛
Alternatively: Opt for Matcha Lattes, herbal teas, ceremonial grade cacao, Chai Lattes. Try it for a week and see if you can feel the difference. 

If you find you are waking with no energy and feel like you need coffee throughout the day it might be best to check with your health specialist whether that’s your GP Acupuncturist or Naturopath for some blood testing and see if there is any underlying deficiency causing the way you are feeling.

DVt-eOzE8k-.content:
I feel like I’ve been saying this time and time again to people recently. 
Did you know that by having your tea/coffee as the first thing you drink/eat for the day actually doesn’t support helping to keep you functional in the day? Here’s why: 

If you’re someone having your supplements with your tea/coffee first thing in the morning you’re actually preventing essential vitamins and minerals from being absorbed in the body from both supplement and food sources. 

Tea and Coffees contain polyphenols and tannins that bind to iron in the gut 
forming complexes your body can’t absorb. This mainly affects non-heme iron (the type in plant foods and most supplements). Drinking tea or coffee with iron can reduce absorption between 40–80% of both heme based and non heme based iron. 

If you then add cows milk, it can make it worse for iron because milk contains  calcium which competes with iron for absorption in the intestine by another 20-40%.
Other supplements such as vitamin D, zinc and magnesium are also affected by milk based tea/coffee drinks but not as significantly as iron. Still if you’re on a list of supplements that you need to support your body for your concern, separating the time between your meals & supplements with the time you have that first tea/coffee if key. Try and wait at least 2 hours between meal and supplement consumption and also pair your supplement intake with vitamin C especially for iron absorption.

Additionally drinking caffeine on an empty stomach increases cortisol (your stress hormone) and further triggers a blood sugar spike. This happens because caffeine stimulates the release of adrenaline and signals the liver to release glucose into the bloodstream. For some people, this can lead to:
• energy crashes later in the day
• increased cravings for sugar or carbs
• feeling jittery or anxious
• disrupted appetite and mood
A simple fix: is food that is high in protein, fibre and healthy fats FIRST. This helps slow glucose release and keeps your energy more stable throughout the day.

5 Ways to Protect Your Peace ✨

1. Set Boundaries – Prioritize your well-being by saying no or staying away from people/ places that drain your energy.
2. Practice Mindfulness – Take time to meditate, reflect, or just be present in the moment.
3. Surround Yourself with Positivity – Keep uplifting people and environments around you. This will draw-out the negative and bring in the positive.
4. Disconnect to Reconnect – Step away from social media and technology when you need a mental break.
5. Self-Care is a Must – Make time for activities that relax and recharge you. Feeling good starts from with in!

CiTcrSHvwg_.content:
In honor of world suicide day….
I have lost friends and family to suicide …. Forever in our hearts …

 She found herself on the floor of her bedroom clutching the belt and the coat hanger…
She got lucky…

She crashed her car and stepped away unharmed, 
More than once….
An angel must of intervened, 

She stood looking over the edge contemplating how quickly life could end, 
But an eagle caught her eye , 

She lost her dreams , 
And her demons almost won , 
But kind words told her to keep going , 

She persevered, 
And had people try and cut her down, 
She almost choked, 
But family were strong by her side to lift her spirits, 

She doesn’t know how she’s still here, 
She doesn’t know what will keep fanning her flames ….

But she knows she’s part of something bigger …playing her part and part of the chink in a much bigger web of love .. 

She wants you to know her heart, 
She doesn’t need to hide, 

There is another chapter she’s working on that needs another chance , 
She is scared but deep down she knows it’s the right time …..

You never know what someone is fighting…

So, if you can be anything in this world,  be kind…

#worldsuicideday2022

Ghee originated in India and has been used there for thousands of years.

Ghee is cultured, clarified butter (the milk solids and water are removed leaving just the fat). 

Ayurvedically, ghee is used extensively in cooking and therapeutic applications, both internally and externally, as the best medium for delivering Ayurvedic formulations.

- Aids digestion 

- Is nourishing, strengthening, immunity building

- Is anti-inflammatory and rich in linoleic acid, Vitamins (A, K2, and E), and Omega-3 fatty acids. And it’s a source of butyrate acid, a short-chain fatty acid that promotes gut health.

- Heals the gut and supports the liver, heart, and kidneys

- It is good for mental health conditions, and improves brain health, concentration, cognitive function, intelligence, and memory.

** Although a source of dairy, it is very well tolerated by many people intolerant to dairy due to the milk solids being removed.

DUWpqG8k6og.content:
I’ll go back to my nest now please 🪹

Resuming life as usual again can be overwhelming for both mama and babe.

I find it hard to talk about this time… beyond 6 weeks… because I feel like we are already fighting for people to acknowledge the first 6 weeks at all.

But just because you’ve landed at 6 weeks doesn’t mean everything has now changed and life goes back to normal. 

There is an adjustment that comes at this stage too. 

You’re still waking multiples times a night, you are likely leaking milk and struggling to shower by midday. Your nervous system is on high alert and going out into the world can feel overwhelming. 

Things like car rides can be awful when your baby doesn’t like the car. 

This is what I like to call the symphony of stress with twins. 

Timing car rides so both babies are fed, settled and happy can be impossible. Especially if you have somewhere to be.

So if you are emerging from postpartum, it’s okay to not have it together. To feel overwhelmed or nervous. 

Some mamas are up and out and really not affected by this transition. It’s amazing. But I know that’s not a reality for most. 

Here’s a reminder that you aren’t alone. Take it slow - baby steps.

You are still in your fourth trimester.

DVUj01qE3vP.content:
5 things I didn’t do in the first 5 days postpartum 

🛌 I didn’t leave my bed

Being in bed facilitates rest. It becomes your safe space. Your nest.

It’s where healing happens. Where you prioritise skin to skin and feed around the clock without distraction. Away from the visual pull of everything that “needs” doing.

Five days in the bed, five days on the bed, five days around the bed — the 5/5/5 rule should be a bare minimum.

🥗 I didn’t eat cold or raw food or drink cold drinks

Warmth supports healing. After birth your body is repairing tissue, rebalancing hormones, establishing milk supply, restoring blood.

Cold food requires more digestive effort when your body needs to prioritise recovery.

Warm broths, stewed fruit, congee and slow-cooked meals support circulation and digestion without adding extra work.

🚿 I didn’t wash my hair

There is something powerful about the natural scent of early postpartum — the warm, milky smell of your body and your baby.

Oxytocin is heightened in those early days and scent plays a role in bonding. Strong fragrances can mask those natural cues. The same applies to scented body wash, deodorant and perfumes. Especially in those early days, be mindful of synthetic fragrances — and gently share that with visitors too.

🧣 I didn’t let my belly go unsupported

After birth your organs are finding their way back into place. Everything feels open and tender.

Wrapping the belly provides containment, eases discomfort and supports healing.

🛁 I didn’t bath my babies

Babies aren’t dirty. They arrive coated in vernix, which supports their skin barrier and early microbiome.

Delaying bathing supports temperature stability and breastfeeding initiation. In those early days, skin to skin and sleepy warmth matter most.

🪺🫧🕊️

DVw9N_EEjRP.content:
11 weeks 🌞

This last week has been heavy and hard.

It’s rare for mum guilt to take over me like this. To find myself breaking down in tears again and again. Today feels a little lighter though. I’m not completely through it yet, but I feel like I have more of a plan.

Feeding babies can be SO hard. It feels strange saying that at the 11 week mark with my second set of twins and another beautiful daughter who were all exclusively breastfed until well over two.

But just like each of our babies are different, we can be different each time too. Our bodies change. Sometimes that shows up in beautiful ways, and other times it can be incredibly challenging. This can play out in pregnancy, birth, and motherhood. 

I’m working through it with amazing support and love from the village. Another way the village shows up long after the six weeks are done. I have mamas pumping and delivering me their milk, and professional villagers guiding me through. We’ve got this. But when your milk slows and your babies need you, it feels awful.

I wanted to share because if you’ve been here, or if you are here, you’re not alone.

And also because this is the fourth trimester. It’s why I love that term so much. Because it reminds us that everything doesn’t suddenly stop or get easy at the six week mark. None of this is linear either.

Not that everything magically resolves at three months either, but it gives mamas more time. More time to land. More time to find their feet.

I don’t believe in ‘postpartum is forever’. Yes, you are forever changed when you become a mother, but you are not stuck in postpartum forever. That idea can feel overwhelming and unhelpful for mothers. Matrescence is the transition, the lifelong change that follows.

But six weeks isn’t enough.

The Fourth Trimester matters ❣️

DWBdw4tJqme.content:
It’s Multiple Awareness Week and this ain’t my first rodeo 😅🤠

As a mama of two sets of twins and a slightly crunchy twin mama trying to challenge the way we approach twin motherhood…

These are the hills I’d die on:

✌🏽Not all twins come early. I went over 41 weeks with both sets. All four arrived beautifully healthy and we didn’t need special care or NICU time. I don’t believe we should be cutting twins out early just because “twins come early” or “my doctor said.” Always ask why.

✌🏽And on that… you can birth twins vaginally and in water. Being told you’re “not allowed” to do something when it isn’t medically necessary doesn’t sit right with me. It’s your body and your babies. Assuming all is well, you can absolutely birth without an epidural, in water, vaginally.

✌🏽Twin babies are still babies, not robots. Syncing them into strict routines is wild to me. Two completely different little people with their own personalities, needs, sleep patterns, and feeding rhythms. Embrace rhythm over rigid routine. Learn your babies instead of trying to force them to be the same. 

✌🏽You don’t need two of everything. You don’t need double the stuff just because it’s twins. More things don’t always make it easier. Keep it simple and marketplace is your best friend.

✌🏽You can absolutely bed share and enjoy sleep in your first year of twins. I don’t get up once over night with my twins. Because we are all together feeding, co regulating, sleeping and rousing the way we are designed to. 

✌🏽You can breastfeed twins. You don’t have to formula feed “just to survive.” It’s not always easy, but it is absolutely possible. Support makes all the difference.

✌🏽You can love being a twin mum, adore your babies, and still long for easier days.Amongst the beauty there is chaos. Amongst the tears and overwhelm, there is the most incredible gift.Twins are the biggest blessing.

I won the lottery twice. 

#twins #twinmum #twinstwice #crunchytwins

DYjFRkwCauM.content:
Top 5 tips for graduating nappies 🐨🚽

The OG twins are finally graduating out of nappies and honestly… toilet training twins felt incredibly daunting.

Every child is so different. My daughter practically toilet trained herself at 2, while the boys showed absolutely no signs of readiness at that age. So I left it and decided to tackle it over summer instead.

And truly, if you can time it for summer, do it! Less layers, more outside time, and easy nappy-free moments make it so much easier.

We always focus on daytime first, then nighttime usually follows a little later.

Here are my biggest toilet training tips:

1. Wait until they’re ready
Don’t force it. You don’t want stress, fear, or pressure around toileting. It becomes so much easier when they’re interested and involved. Every little bum is different, there’s no rush. My twins were months apart in readiness!

2. Put undies in the nappy drawer
Such a simple shift, but it helps create a new rhythm. Instead of automatically reaching for a nappy, offer “big kid” undies instead. It doesn’t take many accidents before they start becoming more aware of their body and cues.

3. Get a kids toilet seat
Toilets can feel huge and intimidating for little people. We skipped the potty and went straight to a toilet seat insert to avoid double training. The built-in magnetic kids seats from Bunnings are so good and made a huge difference to confidence. 

4. Waterproof sheets are essential
Night training can take a little longer and accidents are completely normal. Waterproof sheets make the whole process so much less stressful. I love @organicpeach_ and @spewyau 

5. A flexible nappy subscription helps so much
Toilet training is unpredictable. Some weeks you fly through nappies, other weeks barely any. Having a flexible subscription you can pause or stop anytime makes the whole transition feel much more seamless and less wasteful.

DYn4AARiRri.content:
There’s something I’ve been building over the past 40 days. 

Because like so many mothers right now, I’ve been trying to work out what; work, motherhood and modern life can actually look like together.

I’ve spent years thinking about this idea.

And over the past month, while feeding babies around the clock, I finally started bringing it to life.

There’s so much noise around AI at the moment.

People love it.
People hate it.
People think it’s going to take jobs or take over the world.

But honestly, it’s given me an opportunity that I don’t take for granted. 

The ability to stay with my babies. 

Right now, it’s opening doors that simply didn’t exist before.

It’s giving people access to tools, skills and possibilities that once felt completely out of reach unless you had huge budgets, endless time, childcare, support or an entire team behind you.

And I think there’s something really special about that in the hands of mothers.

Women who are deeply capable and deeply inspired, but also time poor, under slept, touched out and trying to build things in the corners of their lives.

My new baby launches next week.

DYqqwaTJ--R.content:
Yes, we talk a lot about the lack of postpartum support.

But there’s another side to it we don’t speak about enough.

Mothers can be their own worst enemy when it comes to accepting help.

Most people say “let me know if you need anything,” but that support is often hard to turn into action.

And not always because people don’t show up.

Sometimes because mothers struggle to actually put the call out. Or even say yes when help is offered.

“Oh no, I’m fine.”
“It’s okay, I can handle it.”

And yes, absolutely you can.

You’re a mother.
You can do anything.

But postpartum was never meant to be about proving how much you can carry.

It’s supposed to be a season of resting, recovering and replenishing.

And anything that pulls you away from that is pulling you away from exactly where you need to be.

I think so many women struggle to receive support because it’s in our nature to nurture.
To care for others.
To keep going.
To not inconvenience anyone.

You know the whole, people pleasing, good girl in all of us.

I want to change that.

Comment GATHER to join the waitlist for my new baby 🌀

DM64xFdTN1C.content:
I don’t know where Liddle came from but I’m so glad he took shelter in my bushes. 
He was there when we moved in… this little cat with a stumpy tail and little legs. He was terrified of humans and would hiss if we went near him. 
I started to feed him and he began coming out of the bush and hanging out our door. For around a year and a half I made sure there was food and water for him and a bed outside. 
When we decided to move out, I knew I couldn’t just abandon him. He relied on me and trusted me. 
I brought him inside to get him ready to find his forever home. We found out he had FIV and even with the help of a rescue no one wanted him. He had bad skin, a bad attitude and required too much work and patience. 
That’s when I knew that he was mine. I loved him so much but with a baby and 2 cats already I thought I couldn’t possibly keep him! The universe showed me otherwise. 
Liddle was my biggest project, everyday I’d spend big chunks of time just gaining his trust and love. He was there everyday when my mum was sick in hospital and after she passed. Dedicating time to him helped ease my pain. He was always there for me. I will never forget that. So I will always be there for him ❤️❤️❤️🐱🐈

#catrescue #straycat #fiv #catlover #cattransformation

Did you see real tired signs?

Not one yawn.
A cluster of tired signs.
Yawning, rubbing eyes, looking away, maybe red eyebrows.

Undertired can look peaceful.
Rolling. Babbling. Kicking around happy.

It can also look messy.
Crying because they weren’t done.
Sometimes they’re just bored. Those signs look a lot like tired signs.

People call that overtired. It’s usually not.

Dysregulated feels different.
You can see the upset.
They’re hard to settle.
Everything escalates.
That often shows up after long wake windows, hectic days, or big feelings that never got cleared.

Here’s the part that makes bedtime finally make sense.

Calm with no tired signs: add ten to fifteen minutes extra before bedtime tomorrow.

Upset with no tired signs: slow the lead up. More connection. They may still need extra wake time.

Clear tired signs plus dysregulation: shorten the last stretch or bring bedtime forward next time.

Watch the pattern.
That’s what tells the truth.

When you read cues and timing together, bedtime stops feeling like a mystery.
You know what move to make.

Save this for the next bedtime that drags.

Your baby rubs their eyes.

Then starts yawning. Maybe fussing a little.

Tired cues don’t come one at a time.
They come in a group.

Things like:
↓ Eye rubs or red eyebrows
↓ Looking away/disengaging
↓ Fussing
↓ Yawning
↓ Staring into space

The thing is, one cue on its own could be anything. 

Like, “my eye is itchy”, or “I’m bored of this”.

Multiple cues together?
That’s your window.

And here’s the test: if you offer a new activity and the cues disappear, they weren’t truly tired yet. They might have just wanted to do something new.

If the cues stay, that’s telling you it’s time for sleep.

The wake window chart can’t tell you when that cluster will appear.

Only your baby can!

We added 20 minutes to his wake windows. Watched for clusters instead of single cues. Within a week he went from waking every hour to 4 hour stretches.

Your baby’s biology doesn’t care what the chart says they should need.

Comment STARTERKIT and I’ll send you my free checklist of what to actually check before changing how you’re settling.

DYsmp8RElJn.content:
Feeding your baby to sleep doesn’t create a bad habit. It creates a fed, sleeping baby.

The ‘bad habit’ narrative comes from sleep training culture, where independent sleep is usually the goal and anything involving you is framed as a problem you need to fix.

But sleep associations are just the conditions present when your baby falls asleep. Feeding. Rocking. Contact. Darkness. White noise. They’re all associations (we all have them!) - and they’re neutral until they stop working for your family.

That’s the only test that matters. Not whether somebody else says it’s wrong. Whether it’s sustainable for YOU.

Babies who feed to sleep don’t stay that way forever. They will usually naturally transition as they develop, as overnight feeding needs drop, as they mature. You’re not locking them into a pattern for life. 

If feeding to sleep is working and you’re both getting rest, keep going. If it’s stopped working or you’re exhausted, or you just can’t do it anymore, we can change it gently without cutting off comfort or connection.

You can feed your baby to sleep AND work toward easier nights. Those two things can co-exist while you figure out what actually works for your baby.

And if you want support with this? I’m here 🫶
